# Risk and Return Attribution

## Where Week 07 Left Off

Week 07 built portfolios.

This week takes one apart and asks where its risk and its return actually came
from.

That is the question anyone who has to explain a quarter to a client is being
asked.

::: {.notes}
Two exercises, same machinery run in opposite directions. Attribution takes a
portfolio and allocates its risk and return to the pieces. Risk budgeting picks
the allocation of risk first and solves for the portfolio. Both rest on one
fact about homogeneous functions.
:::

## Ex-Post and Ex-Ante

Attribution finds the contribution to return or risk from underlying factors.

**Ex-post** looks at realized risk and return. How much did this stock add to
the total return, and to the realized standard deviation?

**Ex-ante** looks at assumed forward distributions and finds the contributions to
expected risk and return.

## The Decomposition

Estimate the first derivative and use

$$
f(x) \approx \sum_{i}^{n} x_i \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}
$$

Each term is one input's contribution to the total.

## Euler's Theorem

If $f$ is homogeneous of degree 1, $f(\lambda x) = \lambda f(x)$, then

$$
f(x) = \sum_{i}^{n} x_i \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}
$$

exactly, with no error term.

## Both Risk Measures Qualify

Positive homogeneity is the property from Week 05 and Week 07.

Portfolio standard deviation and expected shortfall are both homogeneous of
degree 1 in the weights.

The contributions add to the total exactly. Any residual in your code is an
arithmetic error, not a modeling one.

## Return Attribution

The portfolio return is the sum of the weights times the arithmetic returns:

$$
R_t = \sum_{i}^{n} r_{i,t} w_{i,t}
$$

The derivative with respect to $r_i$ is just the weight. The contribution of
factor $i$ at time $t$ is $w_i r_i$.

## Why Arithmetic Returns

Week 04: arithmetic returns are additive across assets inside a period.

That is exactly what an attribution needs.

# Linking Through Time

## Returns Do Not Add Across Time

The same arithmetic returns are not summable across periods.

The total return is not the sum of the period returns, so the total attribution
is not the sum of the period contributions.

We need a way to link them. The most straightforward is Cariño's K.

## Cariño's K

The arithmetic and geometric total returns:

$$
R = \left[ \prod_{t}^{T} \left( 1 + R_t \right) \right] - 1,
\qquad
GR = \ln(R + 1)
$$

Their ratio:

$$
K = \frac{GR}{R}
$$

## A Scale for Every Period

$$
k_t = \frac{\ln\left( R_t + 1 \right)}{K R_t}
$$

By construction,

$$
R = \sum_{t}^{T} R_t k_t
$$

## Check It Once by Hand

Substitute $k_t$:

$$
\sum_{t}^{T} R_t k_t = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{t}^{T} \ln\left( 1 + R_t \right)
$$

The sum of logs is the log of the product, and the log of the product is $GR$.

$$
\frac{GR}{K} = R
$$

## Attribution for Each Factor

Inside a period the components are summable:

$$
R = \sum_{t}^{T} k_t \sum_{i}^{n} w_{i,t} r_{i,t}
$$

So the total attribution for factor $i$ is

$$
A_i = \sum_{t}^{T} k_t w_{i,t} r_{i,t}
$$

## The Weights Drift

Unless the portfolio is rebalanced every period, the weights move with the
market.

Grow each weight by its return:

$$
w_{i,t}^{*} = w_{i,t}\left( 1 + r_{i,t} \right)
$$

## Normalize

The portfolio return falls out of the grown weights:

$$
R_t = \left( \sum_{i}^{n} w_{i,t}^{*} \right) - 1
$$

Normalize to get the next period's starting weight:

$$
w_{i,t+1} = \frac{w_{i,t}^{*}}{R_t + 1}
$$

One pass gives both the portfolio returns and the weights at every period.

## Do Not Skip It

A position that doubles while the rest of the book is flat carries a very
different weight at the end than at the start.

Attributing its later returns at the original weight misstates every line of the
report.

And it does so without any error large enough to notice.

# Risk Attribution

## Volatility as the Risk

$$
\sigma_p = \sqrt{w'\Sigma w}
$$

The gradient:

$$
\frac{\partial \sigma_p}{\partial w} = \frac{\Sigma w}{\sqrt{w'\Sigma w}}
$$

For an individual $w_i$, take the $i^{th}$ row.

## Component Volatility

$$
CSD = w\, \#\, \frac{\Sigma w}{\sqrt{w'\Sigma w}}
$$

$\#$ is element wise multiplication.

By Euler, the components sum to $\sigma_p$.

## What CSD Is Not

It is not the risk of holding position $i$ on its own.

The components do not add to the sum of the individual volatilities. They add to
the portfolio volatility, the smaller number.

The difference is diversification. The gradient allocates it across the
positions instead of leaving it as an unexplained residual.

## The Gradient Is a Covariance

$$
\frac{\partial \sigma_p}{\partial w_i} = \frac{1}{\sigma_p}\sum_{j}^{n}\left( w_j \Sigma_{i,j} \right)
$$

The sum is the definition of $\operatorname{cov}(x_i, p)$, so

$$
RA_i = \frac{w_i \operatorname{cov}(x_i,p)}{\sigma_p} = \frac{\operatorname{cov}(w_i x_i, p)}{\sigma_p}
$$

## It Is a Regression

The OLS $\beta$ from Week 02:

$$
\beta = \frac{\operatorname{cov}(y, x)}{\sigma_x^2}
$$

Regress the weighted returns on the portfolio return:

$$
w_i x_i = c + \beta_{i,p}\, p + \epsilon
\qquad \Rightarrow \qquad
RA_i = \sigma_p \beta_{i,p}
$$

## Ex-Post Needs Only Returns

Ex-ante risk attribution needs a covariance matrix.

Ex-post needs only a series of realized returns and a regression.

Week 02 machinery, applied to a question Week 02 never asked.

## Beta Is a Share

Divide both sides by $\sigma_p$:

$$
\frac{RA_i}{\sigma_p} = \beta_{i,p}
$$

The beta of position $i$ against the portfolio is its fraction of total
portfolio risk.

A beta of 0.30 is 30% of the volatility, whatever the volatility happens to be.

## The Betas Sum to 1

Regressing the portfolio on itself gives a coefficient of 1.

The regression is linear in its dependent variable, so the individual betas add
to that.

Shares that sum to 1 are shares. It is also a free check on the arithmetic.

# Problem 1

## The Setup

Construct the maximum Sharpe Ratio portfolio for AAPL, MSFT, BRK-B, CSCO, and
JNJ.

Attribute its realized return, then its realized risk, from 1-14 through the end
of February.

The expected returns come from a factor model, not from sample means.

## Expected Returns From Factors

1. Join the Fama French 3 factor file to momentum, divide by 100, join to
   `DailyReturn.csv`
2. Regress each stock on $[\text{Mkt-RF},\ \text{SMB},\ \text{HML},\ \text{Mom}]$
   with an intercept. Keep the betas, discard the intercept
3. Each factor's expected daily return is its mean over the last 10 years
4. Geometric, annualized at 255 days:

$$
\mu_i = 255 \cdot \ln\left( 1 + \sum_{j} \beta_{i,j} E(f_j) \right)
$$

## Covariance From the Stocks

$$
\Sigma = 255 \cdot \operatorname{cov}\left( \ln(1 + Y) \right)
$$

Maximize the Sharpe Ratio subject to $\sum w_i = 1$ and $w_i \geq 0$, at a risk
free rate of 25bp.

A non-linear objective. It needs a solver, not a closed form.

## Why Not a Factor Covariance

We are assuming multivariate normality. A multivariate normal is completely
described by $\mu$ and $\Sigma$.

Splitting $\Sigma$ into a factor covariance and idiosyncratic variances would
only add estimation error to a quantity we can already get in one step.

## $T \gg n$

Five stocks against several years of daily data. $\Sigma$ is full rank and
comfortably estimated.

Every Week 03 concern about singular covariance matrices is absent.

Check that before reusing this setup. As the number of assets approaches the
length of the series, the sample covariance degrades and then fails. That is
Week 09.

| AAPL | 10.076% |

| BRK-B | 43.839% |
| CSCO | 8.118% |

CSCO had the worst total return, $-9.11\%$.

MSFT lost less than half as much, $-3.48\%$, and contributed nearly as much to

## Euler Doing Its Work

The volatility row adds to $1.19\%$, the portfolio volatility.

Not to the sum of the five individual volatilities.

BRK-B had the smallest loss of the five and carried the most risk. Return and risk attribution
answer different questions.

# Attribution to a Factor

## From Positions to Factors

So far, risk and return went to the positions.

Describe each asset with $m$ factors instead:

$$
x_i = \alpha + \beta_i F + \epsilon,
\qquad
\beta_i F = \sum_{j}^{m} \beta_{i,j} F_j
$$

## The Residual

Unless $\alpha = 0$ and $\sigma_e = 0$, the factors will not explain everything.

Collect the error:

$$
e_i = \alpha_i + \epsilon_i
$$

$$
p = \sum_{i}^{n} w_i \sum_{j}^{m} \beta_{i,j} F_j + \sum_{i}^{n} w_i e_i
$$

## Portfolio Alpha

Attribute the error to each asset, or sum it and treat it as one more factor.

In ex-post analysis that total is the portfolio alpha:

$$
\alpha_p = \sum_{i}^{n} w_i e_i
$$

## Two Names, One Residual

**Return side.** Portfolio alpha. The part of the return the factors did not
explain, which is what an active manager is paid for.

**Risk side.** Idiosyncratic, specific, or residual risk. The part of the
volatility that did not come from factor exposure.

Plenty of reports use one term in the return table and the other in the risk
table without saying so. Ask which is meant.

## Collapsing to Factor Weights

Define a factor weight:

$$
w_j = \sum_{i}^{n} w_i \beta_{i,j}
$$

$$
p = \sum_{j}^{m} w_j F_j + \alpha_p
$$

## The Whole Trick

A portfolio of $n$ assets has become a portfolio of $m$ factors plus a residual.

If $m < n$, the problem got smaller.

Nothing after this point knows or cares that the factors are not assets.

## The Recipe

1. Calculate factor weights through time
2. Calculate portfolio return through time
3. Calculate alpha through time
4. Calculate the Cariño K scaling factors
5. Perform the return attribution
6. Regress on the portfolio for the risk attribution

To push the residual back to the assets, expand $\alpha_p = \sum w_i e_i$. The
math is the same.

## Problem 2

Same data as Problem 1.

Attribute realized risk and return to Fama French 3 plus Momentum.

Report the residual total as portfolio alpha.

| | Mkt-RF | SMB | HML | Mom | Alpha | Portfolio |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Total Return | -5.8% | -0.11% | 2.03% | 0.82% | 1.78% | -2.51% |
| Return Attribution | -4.45% | 0 | 0.29% | -0.08% | 1.77% | -2.51% |
| Vol Attribution | 1.00% | -0.01% | -0.07% | 0.01% | 0.27% | 1.19% |

: {tbl-colwidths="[26,13,12,12,12,12,13]"}

Rows are rounded. The underlying attribution sums exactly. Check against the
code, not the printed table.

## The Market Dominates

The market factor accounts for nearly the whole loss and nearly the whole risk.

That is the usual result for a long only equity portfolio.

## Negative Risk Is Not an Error

SMB and HML carry negative volatility attribution.

A factor whose realized returns ran counter to the portfolio reduces total risk.

The gradient gives it a negative share.

# Risk Budgeting and Risk Parity

## Is Optimized Optimal?

Richard Michaud, 1989, "The Markowitz Optimization Enigma: Is 'Optimized'
Optimal?"

Small changes to correlations, volatilities, and expected values change the
portfolio dramatically.

> "Mean Variance Optimization is Error Maximizing."

## Or as Yogi Berra Said

> "It's tough to make predictions, especially about the future."

## The Mechanism Is Week 01

The standard error of an estimated mean is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$.

For returns, $\sigma$ dwarfs $\mu$.

The optimizer takes the noisy means at face value and loads up on whichever
asset happened to look best.

## What We Know Better

Long term plans use estimated returns and covariance. In the long run, risk
premia are fairly stable.

Shorter term, we are less confident about expected return.

We are more confident about volatilities, and to some extent correlations.

## Risk Budgets

Ex-ante risk contributions as a percentage of total risk show how much risk each
position is given.

Without a good view on expected return, control how much risk each position uses
instead.

That is risk budgeting.

## The Max Sharpe Budget

| AAPL | MSFT | BRK-B | CSCO | JNJ |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 11.8% | 29.5% | 39.7% | 9.15% | 9.8% |

: Risk budget implied by the Problem 1 weights

AAPL, CSCO, and JNJ have roughly the same budget.

MSFT has 3x their risk. BRK-B has 4x.

## Money Against Risk

![Share of capital against share of ex-ante risk, maximum Sharpe Ratio portfolio](../figures/money-vs-risk.png){width=72%}

## The Two Views Diverge

BRK-B is 43.8% of the money and 39.7% of the risk. Close.

JNJ is 17.0% of the money and 9.8% of the risk. MSFT is 21.0% of the money and
29.5% of the risk.

When they diverge, the risk view tells you what the portfolio will actually do.

## Risk Parity

Set the risk budgets equal.

$$
CSD = w\, \#\, \frac{\Sigma w}{\sqrt{w'\Sigma w}},
\qquad
SSE = \sum_{i}^{n} \left( CSD_i - \overline{CSD} \right)^2
$$

$$
\min SSE
\qquad
s.t.\ \sum_{i}^{n} w_i = 1
$$

## Least Squares, Non-Linear

It is a least squares problem.

The square root and the inverse of portfolio volatility make it non-linear.

It needs a non-linear optimizer.

## Risk Parity Weights

| Stock | Weight | Risk Budget | $\sigma$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| AAPL | 15.4% | 20% | 25.6% |
| MSFT | 14.3% | 20% | 25.5% |
| BRK-B | 26.5% | 20% | 15.2% |
| CSCO | 15.1% | 20% | 23.4% |
| JNJ | 28.7% | 20% | 14.9% |

: Same covariance matrix as Problem 1 {tbl-colwidths="[28,24,24,24]"}

## Low Risk, Large Weight

Lower risk stocks get larger weights, roughly in proportion to $1/\sigma$.

JNJ has the lowest volatility, 14.9%, and the largest weight, 28.7%.

AAPL at 25.6% volatility takes about half that.

## No Expected Return Anywhere

No expected return appears in the optimization.

No estimated mean can distort the answer.

That is the entire appeal.

## Inverse Volatility

$$
w_i = \frac{1}{\sigma_i} \cdot \frac{1}{\sum_{j}^{n} \frac{1}{\sigma_j}}
$$

An approximation to risk parity.

Good starting values if the optimizer has trouble converging.

## A Chain of Conditions

All correlations equal: risk parity **is** inverse volatility.

All correlations equal and all Sharpe Ratios equal: risk parity is also the
maximum Sharpe Ratio portfolio.

Long term Sharpe Ratios roughly equal: inverse volatility approximates the super
efficient portfolio, with no means or correlations estimated.

## Why It Is Defensible

Not a claim that equal risk shares are inherently right.

Under two assumptions we are more willing to make than a forecast of means,
equal risk shares land on the portfolio the Week 07 optimization would have
chosen.

# Risk Parity with Unequal Risk Budgets

## Expressing a View

Portfolio managers often have an opinion about which assets will outperform.

Give high conviction positions a larger risk budget and low conviction ones a
smaller one.

$$
b = \left[ b_1, b_2,\ \dots,\ b_n \right]
$$

Twice the budget of everything else: $b_2 = 2 b_i \ \ \forall\ i \neq 2$.

## Scale the Components

$$
CSD^{*} = \left[ \frac{CSD_1}{b_1}, \frac{CSD_2}{b_2},\ \dots,\ \frac{CSD_n}{b_n} \right]
$$

$$
SSE = \sum_{i}^{n} \left( CSD_i^{*} - \overline{CSD^{*}} \right)^2,
\qquad
\min SSE \quad s.t.\ \sum_{i}^{n} w_i = 1
$$

## Strictly More General

Set every $b_i$ equal and the division changes nothing.

Plain risk parity is the special case where the manager has no view.

## MSFT 2, JNJ 0.5

| Stock | Weight | Risk Budget | $b$ | RP Weight |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| AAPL | 13.8% | 18.2% | 1 | 15.4% |
| MSFT | 23.2% | 36.4% | 2 | 14.3% |
| BRK-B | 29.1% | 18.2% | 1 | 26.5% |
| CSCO | 14.7% | 18.2% | 1 | 15.1% |
| JNJ | 19.3% | 9.1% | 0.5 | 28.7% |

: High conviction in MSFT, little in JNJ {tbl-colwidths="[22,20,20,14,24]"}

## Counting Shares

$b$ sums to 5.5.

One share is $1/5.5 = 18.2\%$ of the risk. Two shares are $36.4\%$. Half a share
is $9.1\%$.

## Not a Rescaling

BRK-B's risk budget went down, 18.2% against 20%.

Its portfolio weight went up, 29.1% against 26.5%.

Correlations matter.

## The Correlations

| | AAPL | MSFT | BRK-B | CSCO | JNJ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **AAPL**  | 1.00 | 0.61 | 0.00 | 0.20 | (0.08) |
| **MSFT**  | 0.61 | 1.00 | (0.04) | 0.38 | (0.04) |
| **BRK-B** | 0.00 | (0.04) | 1.00 | 0.22 | 0.40 |
| **CSCO**  | 0.20 | 0.38 | 0.22 | 1.00 | 0.17 |
| **JNJ**   | (0.08) | (0.04) | 0.40 | 0.17 | 1.00 |

: Correlation matrix used in the risk parity examples

## Trace It Through

MSFT is correlated 0.61 with AAPL and 0.38 with CSCO. Raising MSFT raises the
risk of two other positions along with its own.

BRK-B and JNJ were offsetting MSFT. JNJ's weight was cut.

BRK-B, at $-0.04$, is the only place to put money without adding to the
concentration just created.

# Non-Normal Risk Parity

## Beyond Volatility

Every risk parity portfolio so far assumed multivariate normality and used
volatility.

Returns are not normal. We need a more robust risk measure.

## VaR Will Not Do

VaR is not coherent.

One implication: the VaR surface is non-convex. Optimizations may not converge,
and can converge to a local optimum that is not the global one.

ES is coherent, and convex.

## Component Expected Shortfall

$$
ES(w) = \sum_{i}^{n} w_i \frac{\partial ES}{\partial w_i}
$$

Euler again. ES is positively homogeneous, property 3 of coherence in Week 05.

The decomposition is exact for the same reason it was exact for volatility.

## No Closed Form

Without a known distribution, ES has no closed form gradient.

Estimate it with a finite difference on the simulated returns $R$:

$$
\frac{\partial ES}{\partial w_i} \approx \frac{ES\left( \left[ w_1,\ \dots,\ w_i + e,\ \dots,\ w_n \right]\ |\ R \right) - ES(w\ |\ R)}{e}
$$

The forward difference from Week 07.

## Hold $R$ Fixed

Use the same simulated return matrix for both evaluations.

The numerator is a difference of two nearly equal numbers.

Redraw $R$ between them and the simulation noise dominates the derivative.

## The Same Optimization

$$
CES = w\, \#\, \frac{\partial ES}{\partial w},
\qquad
SSE = \sum_{i}^{n} \left( CES_i - \overline{CES} \right)^2
$$

$$
\min SSE
\qquad
s.t.\ \sum_{i}^{n} w_i = 1
$$

Only the component risk changed. Divide by $b$ for unequal budgets, as before.

## Problem 3

Same data as Problem 1, assuming a 0 mean return.

Fit a $t$ distribution to each stock.

Simulate the system with a Gaussian copula.

Find the risk parity portfolio using ES as the risk measure.

## ES Against Volatility

| Stock | ES RP Portfolio | Vol RP Portfolio | Fitted DF |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| AAPL | 14.9% | 15.4% | 60,120 |
| MSFT | 13.5% | 14.3% | 4.6 |
| BRK-B | 26.4% | 26.5% | 21.7 |
| CSCO | 14.2% | 15.1% | 4.5 |
| JNJ | 31.0% | 28.7% | 9.4 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,26,26,26]"}

## Fat Tails Lose Weight

AAPL's fitted degrees of freedom are enormous. It is effectively normal here, and
so is BRK-B.

MSFT and CSCO have the lowest degrees of freedom. Both are cut.

Their fat tails contribute more to tail risk.

## Three Risk Parity Portfolios

![Risk parity under equal budgets, unequal budgets, and ES](../figures/risk-parity-weights.png){width=72%}

## The Honest Headline

The differences are small.

Switching from volatility to ES moved the largest weight by 2.3 percentage
points.

Changing the budgets moved JNJ by 9.4.

See the size of the effect before committing to the extra machinery.

## Where This Goes

Every attribution here took the factors as given.

Problem 1 got away with a sample covariance because $T \gg n$.

Week 09 builds the factors, and drops that assumption.
